title: "Trustworthy AI & Data Hackathon: Agentic Assurance"
weight: 0
---

In this hackathon your team runs AI agents that resolve a telco network fault,
and wins by proving to a judge exactly what those agents did. You get an AWS
account with the platform already running; by the end you hand the judges an
Evidence Pack that answers their questions from the records alone.

**Can you prove what your agents did?** Proving it means a judge playing
auditor can answer from your evidence, after the environment has spent a day
and a half working against you. "It worked" is not enough.

::alert[The three reference agents you start with already fail one of the three graded faults. They follow written policy and refuse the trap, but under ambiguity they guess confidently instead of saying what they do not know. Closing that gap is the game.]{header="You start with agents that are good, and provably not good enough" type="warning"}

:::alert{type="info" header="Disclaimer"}
The AI-native ODA Canvas with MoDaaS is a TM Forum Catalyst reference
implementation built on the open ODA Canvas. It is experimental code that
runs on AWS managed services; it is not itself an AWS service and is not covered by AWS Support. Interfaces (CRDs at v1beta1, operator behavior,
cockpit APIs) may change between builds. Use it to learn and to build
hackathon entries; do not run production traffic through it. It is provided
as-is, without warranty of any kind, under the licenses published with this
workshop (MoDaaS core Apache-2.0, workshop glue MIT-0). If you run it outside a
Workshop Studio event, you are responsible for the AWS costs and for
compliance in your own account.
:::

| Already running in your account | Yours to build |
|---|---|
| The **AI-native ODA Canvas** with its governance layer live. Its namespaces and commands carry the name `modaas`; that is the platform. | Agents that resolve network faults *and leave evidence an auditor accepts* |
| Three reference agents (Customer, IT, Network) that negotiate across domains | The judgment they lack: knowing when to gather evidence or escalate instead of acting |
| A tamper-evident audit ledger that records every model call, tool call and decision | Your Evidence Pack, the artifact you are judged on |
| Three graded fault scenarios and a deterministic grader (`score-run.py`) | A passing grade on the fault the reference agents cannot crack |

One command injects a fault. Three governed agents analyze it, negotiate and
decide, and their correlated records land in the ledger. Then you make them
better, and the grader scores the records, not how convincing the prose is.

![Live governance topology: every agent, model and tool call on one screen](/static/images/ui-graph-view.png)

*The cockpit's live governance graph. A thin gray edge is a path that was
declared but never used, which is exactly what an auditor asks about.*

The scenario escalates through three alert levels. At each one you are scored
on what you can prove, not what you claim:

| Alert level | Conditions | You must prove |
|---|---|---|
| **0: Vanilla** | Normal operations | The flow runs, safeguards are active, evidence is correlated end to end |
| **1: Hostile** | Delays, tampered prompts and skills, conflicting context | Detection, safe degradation, unsafe actions denied |
| **2: Rogue** | Bypass attempts, unauthorized tool use, tampered audit records | Containment, evidence preservation, reconstruction |

The judges pick an incident from **your** event window and ask six auditor
questions: who acted, what it touched, whether it was authorized, who
approved it, whether the records kept their integrity, and whether you can
reconstruct the transaction. All six are published up front in
[The Challenge](/challenge-brief).

Target audience: platform, network-automation and security engineers at
communications service providers, and the AWS and partner teams who work with
them. Assumed background: you are comfortable in a Linux terminal, can read
YAML and `kubectl` output, and know what a foundation model and an agent are.
You do not need prior [Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/what-is-bedrock.html)
or ODA Canvas experience.

At the end you will be able to:

- declare a model, tool or agent as a Kubernetes resource and take it through
  admission and human approval before it can serve traffic;
- prove from the audit ledger, gateway logs and
  [Amazon CloudWatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch.html) who called
  which model or tool, and whether the call was allowed;
- build your own agent on
  [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agents-tools-runtime.html) that calls models
  and tools only through the governed gateway;
- hand a judge an Evidence Pack that answers the six auditor questions.

This workshop can only be used at an AWS-run event. It runs in accounts that
AWS Workshop Studio provides and deletes afterwards; there is no self-paced
path in your own account.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Level** | 300 |
| **Duration** | 1.5 days |
| **Region** | us-east-1 only |
| **Cost** | None to you. The event runs in AWS Workshop Studio, which provides the accounts. |
| **Setup** | Nothing to install. Your account arrives with [Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/what-is-eks.html), the ODA Canvas, MoDaaS and the governed gateway deployed, plus a browser IDE. Module 3 has you check each part. |

Work through the pages in the order of the left-hand menu. Each module opens
with what you will do and what you will have at the end, gives numbered steps
with a command, its expected output and what that output proves, and ends with
a **Checkpoint**: one command whose output shows the module worked. Later
modules assume the earlier ones are done, so if a checkpoint fails, fix it
before you move on.

Commands run in your IDE's terminal unless a step says otherwise. Sample
outputs were captured on a real event and are marked with their capture date;
names, ages and ids differ in your account.

Read [Getting Started](/what-to-expect) for the mission, the schedule and the
two rules that protect your event.

title: "Reference: Network Tool Naming"
weight: 72
---

Every tool your agent calls needs a name an agent can act on without reading
your source, and a `ToolConfig` your gateway can govern. This page shows one
convention for the first job and the exact CR shape for the second, so you
can declare a 5G network function as a governed tool instead of a plain
HTTP call your agent trusts blindly. You do not need this page to finish the
[Baseline Walkthrough](/baseline-walkthrough); consult it when you build your
own network-calling tool in [Module 9](/build-your-own-agent).

The [AI Native Networks Immersion Day](https://catalog.workshops.aws/ai-native-networks/en-US)
workshop's [Additional Resources](https://catalog.workshops.aws/ai-native-networks/en-US/module9-additional-resources/module3-agentic-core)
module names 5G core interfaces as callable tools with the shape
`<domain>_<verb>_<resource>`, for example `amf_manage_ue()`,
`smf_create_session()`, `nrf_register_nf()`, `f1_setup_control()`. The
function name is the 3GPP interface reference (`N2`, `N4`, `F1`, `Xn`), so an
agent can tell what a tool does from its name alone, and the tool boundary
matches a real network function boundary rather than an implementation
detail someone chose that day.

| Domain | Function name | 3GPP interface | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core (AMF) | `amf_manage_ue()` | N2 (NGAP) | UE registration and mobility |
| Core (SMF) | `smf_create_session()` | N4 (PFCP) | PDU session establishment |
| Core (NRF) | `nrf_register_nf()` | SBI | Network function registration |
| RAN split | `f1_setup_control()` | F1-C | CU-CP to DU control plane |

Source: AI Native Networks Immersion Day, Additional Resources, "Deploy
End-to-end 5G Network" module.

:::alert{type="info" header="This workshop's reference agents do not follow this convention yet"}
`network-resolution-agent` talks to a mock JSON fault-injection dataset over
plain HTTP (`/handle`, `/negotiate`), not a governed MCP tool. The rest of
this page shows the step from that plain HTTP call to a `ToolConfig` this
platform can admit, approve, pause and audit.
:::

heading_path: Declare a network function as a governed tool
chunks.text:
Any function from the table above becomes a `ToolConfig` the same way
`demo-tool-cedar.yaml` does in [Module 6](/controls-and-policies): only the
endpoint, the credential, and the Cedar policy change. This declares
`smf_create_session()` as a tool your agent can call through the governed
gateway instead of hitting the SMF directly. Save this as
`smf-create-session.yaml` in your workspace (the command below writes it):

heading_path: Declare a network function as a governed tool
chunks.text:
```bash
cat > smf-create-session.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: oda.tmforum.org/v1beta1
kind: ToolConfig
metadata:
  name: smf-create-session
  namespace: components
spec:
  toolName: smf-create-session
  toolType: mcp
  provider: agentCoreGateway
  description: "PDU session establishment via SMF N4/PFCP: smf_create_session()"
  agentCoreGateway:
    gatewayIdentifier: "${MODAAS_GATEWAY_ID}"   # your account's Gateway; the platform exports this variable to your shell
    credentialProviderType: NONE   # replace with your SMF's real auth mode
    mcpServer:
      endpoint: https://your-smf-mcp-endpoint/mcp
      transport: streamable-http
  governance:
    owner: network-team@example.com
    costCenter: network-ops
    dataClassification: internal
    approval:
      required: true
      requiredApprovals: 1
  safety:
    required: true
EOF
```

heading_path: Declare a network function as a governed tool
chunks.text:
`safety.required: true` marks this tool as handling a sensitive action
(establishing a real network session), which is why
`governance.approval.required` is also `true` here: the platform's admission
webhook rejects a safety-required tool that skips the human approval gate,
so you cannot declare this shape and have it silently auto-approve. Add a
`cedarPolicy` scoping which agent identities may call it and under what
conditions, the same pattern proven live on `demo-tool-cedar.yaml`.

Check the shape admits before you point it at a real endpoint:

```bash
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f smf-create-session.yaml
```

Expected output (captured 2026-09-28, dry run against this build's
`ToolConfig` schema):

```text
toolconfig.oda.tmforum.org/smf-create-session created (server dry run)
```

A dry-run `created` line means the CR is admissible: the schema and the
safety/approval rule above both passed. It proves the shape is correct;
declaring the tool for real and approving it is the same two-step flow
[Module 2 Step 7](/platform-access/docs-tool) walks you through for the docs tool.

heading_path: Why this is worth doing, not just naming things
chunks.text:
The AI Native Networks workshop's own text makes the governance case without
using the word: this MCP abstraction turns a static 5G network deployment
into programmable, agentic-controlled infrastructure. Programmable and
agentic-controlled is exactly the surface that needs the guardrails this
platform provides. An agent that can call `smf_create_session()` can also
call it wrong, or from a compromised identity, or maliciously. Declaring it
as a `ToolConfig` instead of a bare HTTP call gets you four things for free:

heading_path: Why this is worth doing, not just naming things
chunks.text:
- **Admission** checks the tool's declared safety posture before it is
  callable at all, the same CEL rule you just proved above.
- **Approval** requires a human attestation, recorded with the approver's
  identity and timestamp, visible in the
  [AWS Agent Registry](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry.html)
  the same way `nrf_register_nf` would be visible in a real NRF service
  catalog.
- **Pause** cuts every agent's access to `smf-create-session` at the
  perimeter. No per-agent
  [IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html)
  change, no redeploy.
- **The audit trail** (this workshop's reference `audit-store`, an
  intent/invocation/result triple keyed on `correlation_id`) means a PDU
  session that should not have been created has a name, a timestamp, and a
  caller identity attached to it.

heading_path: Why this is worth doing, not just naming things
chunks.text:
:::alert{type="info" header="Use it in the hackathon: tool calls are enforcement points too"}
A governed tool call crosses the same gateway a model call does, so every
`tools/call` produces a logged decision your audit store can record. A
resolution run that calls `smf_create_session()` should leave the same
intent, invocation, and result trail a model call leaves, joined on the
run's `correlation_id`. If you are building toward control 7 (event
recording) for the challenge, this is your second enforcement point:
coverage that holds across both a model call and a tool call is stronger
evidence than coverage on model calls alone.
:::

Confirm the ToolConfig CRD still accepts the shape above on your own cluster
before you build against it:

```bash
kubectl explain toolconfig.spec.agentCoreGateway.mcpServer
```

Expected output (captured 2026-09-28):

```text
GROUP:      oda.tmforum.org
KIND:       ToolConfig
VERSION:    v1beta1

FIELD: mcpServer <Object>


DESCRIPTION:
    Lambda ARN or remote http(s) MCP URL. Operator infers Lambda
    vs native-mcpServer vs OpenAPI dispatch from the endpoint.
    Not required if apiGateway/smithyModel/openApiSchema is declared.

FIELDS:
  endpoint	<string>
    <no description>

  transport	<string>
  enum: streamable-http, sse, stdio
    <no description>
```

The `endpoint` and `transport` fields are exactly the two this page's
`ToolConfig` sets under `mcpServer`. If your cluster's schema still lists
them, the sample above will still admit.

Next: [Resources & How-To](/resources) is the map legend for the rest of your
build, including the cockpit views that show a tool like this one once it is
declared.

title: "Step 6: Ask Amazon Q about AWS"
weight: 60
---

In this step you open Amazon Q in the AWS console and learn what it can and
cannot answer here. At the end you have a place to ask general AWS questions,
and you know which questions to take elsewhere so a wrong answer does not cost
you time.

During the event you will hit plain AWS questions (an IAM policy, a
CloudWatch query, a Lambda error) that have nothing to do with this platform.
Amazon Q in the console answers those well. It has never seen this workshop,
so if you ask it about the gateway, the resources you declare or the evidence
records it will answer confidently and wrongly; the workshop's own
`hackathon-helper` agent is for those questions. Knowing which to ask saves
you from chasing a wrong answer under time pressure.

In the AWS console tab, choose the Amazon Q icon in the right-hand sidebar, or
press <kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>Q</kbd> (<kbd>Option</kbd>+<kbd>Q</kbd> on macOS).
Ask it questions about AWS itself, for example:

- "What does `ImagePullBackOff` mean on an [Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/what-is-eks.html) pod?"
- "Which IAM action does `aws codebuild start-build` require?"
- "How do I read an [AWS CloudFormation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html) stack event for a failed resource?"

For IAM actions, the
[Service Authorization Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/service-authorization/latest/reference/reference_policies_actions-resources-contextkeys.html)
is the authoritative list of actions, resources and condition keys per
service; check Amazon Q's answer against it.

**It cannot see your account.** Amazon Q here is not set up to query the
account's resources, so ask it why your pod is pending and you get generic
guidance, not a diagnosis. For your own resources use `kubectl describe` and
the evidence surfaces from [Step 5](/platform-access/api-surface).

**It does not know MoDaaS.** MoDaaS, `ModelConfig`, `ToolConfig`,
`AgentConfig` and the gateway's rules are not in its training data. If it
answers confidently about a MoDaaS field, treat the answer as invented. Use
`kubectl explain`, the documentation tool you set up in the next step, the
[Resources](/resources) page, or a facilitator.

:::alert{type="info" header="Free tier in workshop accounts"}
Workshop accounts have no Amazon Q Developer Pro subscription, so Pro-only
features are unavailable. If the panel returns a permissions error, that is
the environment, not something you did; tell a facilitator and carry on.
:::

Amazon Q answers a general AWS question in the console sidebar, for example
"What is an EKS Pod Identity association?". If the panel will not open, note
it for a facilitator and continue; nothing later depends on it.

Next: [Step 7: Call your first governed tool](/platform-access/docs-tool).

title: "Step 5: Learn the API surface"
weight: 50
---

In this step you learn the four surfaces you use for the rest of the event
and where every governed endpoint comes from. At the end you have a quick
reference for declaring, calling and auditing governed resources, and you
know the one response check that trips people up.

In Step 4 you saw that every model call goes through the governed gateway.
From here on you will use four things over and over: `kubectl` to declare
resources, the gateway's model endpoint, the gateway's tool endpoint, and the
record of every call the gateway keeps. None of their addresses are typed by
hand; the platform publishes each one in a resource's `status` field. This
page shows you where to look, so you never guess a URL, and it warns you about
the one response field that most people misread on day one.

heading_path: 1. Discover endpoints from status, never hardcode them
chunks.text:
Every governed resource publishes its live endpoint in its own status. List
the governed models:

```bash
kubectl get modelconfig -n components \
  -o custom-columns='ALIAS:.spec.alias,PHASE:.status.phase,ENDPOINT:.status.endpoint'
```

Right now the list is empty (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
ALIAS   PHASE   ENDPOINT
```

That is expected: no model is declared yet. You declare the first ones in
[Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough), and from then on this command is how you
find a model's address. If an endpoint is not in a resource's status, it is
not governed, and in this account an ungoverned path returns `AccessDenied`.

This is the whole API you touch during the event:

| Surface | How | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Declare** governed resources | Kubernetes custom resources, group `oda.tmforum.org/v1beta1`, kinds `ModelConfig`, `ToolConfig`, `AgentConfig` | `kubectl apply` in the `components` namespace |
| **Call** a governed model | OpenAI wire format: `POST /v1/chat/completions`, `model` set to the ModelConfig alias, header `Authorization: Bearer $(cat /tmp/modaas-token)` | `http://modaas-agw.agentgateway-system:8081` (inside the cluster) |
| **Call** a governed tool | MCP over HTTP at `/mcp/<alias>` | `http://modaas-agw.agentgateway-system:8080` (inside the cluster) |
| **Read** the evidence | `GET /timeline?cid=<id>` for people, `GET /records?cid=<id>` for JSON lines | `http://audit-store.components:8080` (inside the cluster) |

Models and tools are on different gateway ports: models on 8081, tools on
8080.

heading_path: 3. Read a resource type's schema from the terminal
chunks.text:
You do not need a docs site to see what a resource accepts. `kubectl explain`
prints the schema installed in your cluster:

```bash
kubectl explain modelconfig.spec --recursive | head -20
```

The output starts with the resource's group, kind and version, then its
fields: `access`, `alias`, `awsBedrock` and more, each with its type
(captured 2026-09-29, first lines):

```text
GROUP:      oda.tmforum.org
KIND:       ModelConfig
VERSION:    v1beta1
```

Use `kubectl explain agentconfig.spec.awsAgentCore` the same way when you
reach agents in Module 7.

:::alert{type="warning" header="A blocked request still returns HTTP 200"}
When a guardrail blocks a prompt, the gateway still answers `200`, as the
OpenAI wire format does. The block is in the body: `finish_reason` is
`content_filter`, the message content is `Input blocked by policy.` and
`usage.total_tokens` is `0`, because the prompt never reached the model. A
check that reads only the HTTP status passes a blocked call. Assert on
`finish_reason == "content_filter"` or on zero tokens instead. You trigger a
block yourself in Module 5.
:::

```bash
kubectl api-resources --api-group=oda.tmforum.org | grep -E 'modelconfigs|toolconfigs|agentconfigs'
```

All three governed resource types are listed (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
agentconfigs              ac               oda.tmforum.org/v1beta1   true         AgentConfig
modelconfigs              mc               oda.tmforum.org/v1beta1   true         ModelConfig
toolconfigs               tc               oda.tmforum.org/v1beta1   true         ToolConfig
```

Next: [Step 6: Ask Amazon Q about AWS](/platform-access/amazon-q).

title: "Step 3: Connect to the cluster"
weight: 30
---

In this step you point `kubectl` at your team's EKS cluster and list its
nodes. At the end every `kubectl` command in the workshop talks to your
cluster, and you have seen the three nodes the platform runs on.

The platform you are about to use is installed in a Kubernetes cluster in
your account. Everything you declare in this workshop (a model, a tool, an
agent) is a Kubernetes resource, and `kubectl` is the command you use to
create it, approve it, pause it and read its status. If `kubectl` is not
talking to your cluster, every later step fails with the same confusing
error, so this step costs one minute and prevents that.

The IDE already has a kubeconfig entry for the cluster. Refreshing it costs
nothing and fixes the one case where it is missing (for example after you
switch to CloudShell).

heading_path: 1. Find the cluster and write the kubeconfig entry
chunks.text:
The guard in this block matters: if cluster discovery returns nothing, the
next command would build a malformed endpoint and fail with a confusing
`Invalid endpoint` error.

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
CLUSTER=$(aws eks list-clusters --region "$REGION" --query 'clusters[0]' --output text)
if [ -z "$CLUSTER" ] || [ "$CLUSTER" = "None" ]; then
  echo "No EKS cluster visible in $REGION. Check you are in the workshop account and in us-east-1." >&2
else
  aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION"
  kubectl get nodes
fi
```

The IDE prints `Updated context` (CloudShell prints `Added new context`),
then the three nodes (captured 2026-09-29; node names and ages differ in
your account, and the patch version and build suffix are shown as `x`):

heading_path: 1. Find the cluster and write the kubeconfig entry
chunks.text:
```text
Updated context arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:<account>:cluster/a-01-eks-cluster-modaas in /home/ec2-user/.kube/config
NAME                            STATUS   ROLES    AGE    VERSION
ip-10-42-128-137.ec2.internal   Ready    <none>   127m   v1.36.x-eks-xxxxxxx
ip-10-42-154-82.ec2.internal    Ready    <none>   127m   v1.36.x-eks-xxxxxxx
ip-10-42-160-198.ec2.internal   Ready    <none>   127m   v1.36.x-eks-xxxxxxx
```

Three `Ready` nodes on Kubernetes 1.36 means the cluster is healthy. Compare
the minor version (`1.36`), not the whole string: the patch level and build
suffix are whatever
[EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/kubernetes-versions.html)
currently ships.

```bash
kubectl get nodes --no-headers | grep -c ' Ready '
```

It prints `3`.

Next: [Step 4: Get your gateway credential](/platform-access/gateway-credential).

---
title: "Step 7: Call your first governed tool"
weight: 70
---

In this step you deploy a documentation search tool, declare it as a governed
`ToolConfig`, approve it, and call it through the gateway. At the end you can
search the ODA Canvas and MoDaaS documentation from your terminal, and you
have walked the full lifecycle every tool you build today goes through:
declare, review, approve, call.

It goes through the same perimeter, admission gate and human approval as
anything you build. Governance comes from where you connect.

The tool is a small MCP server plus a gzipped search index, both mounted from
ConfigMaps, so there is no image to build. The index is split into one shard
per source because a ConfigMap holds at most about 1 MiB. The pod cannot fetch
the index itself: the `components` NetworkPolicy from
[Step 4](/platform-access/gateway-credential) gives it no route to S3.

Download the server, the index and the splitter, and split the index:

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/kb/modaas-docs-mcp.py" source=s3}' -o /tmp/kb-server.py
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/kb/index.py" source=s3}' -o /tmp/kb-index.py
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/kb/index.json" source=s3}' -o /tmp/kb-index.json
python3 /tmp/kb-index.py --split /tmp/kb-index.json /tmp/kb-shards
```

The splitter prints one line per shard and `shards written to /tmp/kb-shards`
(chunk counts change as the docs change; four shards, about 1 036 chunks
total).

Create the ConfigMaps and the deployment, and wait for it:

```bash
kubectl create configmap modaas-docs-mcp-app -n components \
  --from-file=server.py=/tmp/kb-server.py --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply --server-side -f -
for f in /tmp/kb-shards/*.json.gz; do
  shard=$(basename "$f" .json.gz)
  kubectl create configmap "modaas-docs-index-$shard" -n components \
    --from-file="$shard.json.gz=$f" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply --server-side -f -
done
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/kb/modaas-docs-mcp.yaml" source=s3}' | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout status deploy/modaas-docs-mcp -n components --timeout=240s
```

It ends with `deployment "modaas-docs-mcp" successfully rolled out`. The
rollout is the check: the server's `/healthz` returns `503` until an index
shard has loaded, so a pod without its index never becomes Ready and the
rollout fails here instead of every search failing later.

:::alert{type="info" header="Why --server-side"}
Client-side `kubectl apply` stores a full copy of the object in an annotation,
and annotations are capped at 256 KiB. The largest shard would exceed that and
be rejected with `metadata.annotations: Too long`. Server-side apply avoids
the annotation and can still be re-run safely.
:::

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/crs/modaas-docs-toolconfig.yaml" source=s3}' -o /tmp/modaas-docs.yaml
kubectl apply -f /tmp/modaas-docs.yaml
kubectl wait toolconfig/modaas-docs -n components --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}' --timeout=60s 2>/dev/null || true
kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components \
  -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,ENDPOINT:.status.endpoint'
```

The tool is accepted and parked for review (captured 2026-09-29; your load
balancer host differs):

```text
NAME          PHASE       ENDPOINT
modaas-docs   Reviewing   http://<elb-host>:8080/mcp/modaas-docs
```

`Reviewing` is the admission gate at work. The resource declares
`governance.approval.required: true`, so until a person attests to it the
gateway has no route to call. The endpoint is published already, on the
gateway's public load balancer, but it answers only once the tool is
`Approved`.

Approval is two annotations: who approved and what they checked.

```bash
kubectl -n components annotate toolconfig modaas-docs \
  modaas.tmforum.org/approver="$(whoami)@team" \
  modaas.tmforum.org/approval-attestation="Reviewed: public docs corpus, read-only, no egress from the pod" \
  --overwrite
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  PHASE=$(kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}')
  echo "phase=$PHASE"
  [ "$PHASE" = "Approved" ] && break
  sleep 5
done
```

The loop prints `phase=Reviewing` a number of times, then `phase=Approved`.
On the capture event that took about 80 seconds.

:::alert{type="info" header="If the phase stays Reviewing"}
The annotation keys must be exact, including the `modaas.tmforum.org/`
prefix. A mistyped key is not an error, just not an approval, so the tool
stays in `Reviewing` with no message. Re-run the annotate command, then check
that `kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components -o
jsonpath='{.status.governance.approvals}'` shows your name.
:::

MCP is a session protocol: the first request is `initialize`, the server
returns a session id in the `Mcp-Session-Id` response header, and every later
request carries that id. The probe runs in a throwaway pod so the credential
stays inside your cluster; the public endpoint above is plain HTTP, so calling
it from outside would send the token unencrypted.

The block first defines `incluster`, which runs a pod, waits for it to
finish and prints its output once (`kubectl run --rm -i` attaches after the
pod starts, so a short request can finish and print nothing). The same
helper is on your IDE's PATH, so later modules call it from any terminal.

```bash
incluster() {  # incluster NAME [kubectl-run flags] -- COMMAND : run it in a throwaway pod, print its output once
  local p=$1; shift
  kubectl delete pod "$p" -n default --ignore-not-found >/dev/null
  kubectl run "$p" --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.5.0 -n default "$@" >/dev/null || return
  for _ in $(seq 300); do
    case $(kubectl get pod "$p" -n default -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}') in Succeeded|Failed) break;; esac
    sleep 1
  done
  kubectl logs "$p" -n default
  kubectl delete pod "$p" -n default --wait=false >/dev/null
}

TOKEN=$(cat /tmp/modaas-token)
incluster kb-probe --env="TOKEN=$TOKEN" -- sh -c '
U=http://modaas-agw.agentgateway-system:8080/mcp/modaas-docs
MCP_ACCEPT="Accept: application/json, text/event-stream"
# 1. initialize: the server hands back a session id in a response header
SID=$(curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X POST "$U" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "$MCP_ACCEPT" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":0,\"method\":\"initialize\",\"params\":{\"protocolVersion\":\"2025-03-26\",\"capabilities\":{},\"clientInfo\":{\"name\":\"kb-probe\",\"version\":\"1\"}}}" \
  | tr -d "\r" | sed -n "s/^[Mm]cp-[Ss]ession-[Ii]d: //p")
echo "session: ${SID:-NONE - check the token and that modaas-docs is Approved}"
# 2. every later call carries that id
curl -s -X POST "$U" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SID" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "$MCP_ACCEPT" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":1,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"search_docs\",\"arguments\":{\"query\":\"how does the gateway mediate agent calls\",\"limit\":3}}}"
echo'
```

The output starts with `session:` and a long id, then an `event: message`
line and a JSON result. The top hit (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
"source_path": "ai-canvas/decision-log/ADR-004-gateway-mediation-architecture.md",
"heading_path": ["Decision"],
```

Every result carries `source_path` and `heading_path`. The tool never writes
an answer of its own; it returns passages and says where they came from, so
you can open the file behind any claim you make to a judge. Pass an `id` from
the results to `get_doc` for the full passage, or a `source_path` for the
whole document.

| Tool | Arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `search_docs` | `query`, optional `limit` (1 to 20), optional `source` (`ai-canvas`, `modaas`, `oda-canvas`, `workshop`) | Ranked passages, each with `id`, `source_path`, `heading_path`, `score` |
| `get_doc` | `id` (a chunk id from `search_docs`) or a `source_path` | That passage, or the whole file in order |

The index is built only from public sources, each at a pinned commit: the TM
Forum [`oda-canvas`](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/oda-canvas) design docs
and operator READMEs, the TM Forum
[`ai-canvas-architecture`](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/ai-canvas-architecture)
decision log, the MoDaaS resource definitions as published in
[`model-as-a-service-crds`](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/model-as-a-service-crds),
and this workshop's own pages. The published definitions can trail the ones
installed in your cluster; for the exact schema you run, `kubectl explain` is
the authority. [Resources](/resources) describes how the index is built.

:::alert{type="warning" header="The same tool, reached two ways"}
The backend is an ordinary pod, so `kubectl port-forward deploy/modaas-docs-mcp
-n components 8080:8080` and a direct `POST /mcp` also work, with no
credential, no policy decision and nothing for an auditor to see.
`/mcp/modaas-docs` on the gateway is the governed door; the pod's own address
is a side entrance. Closing side entrances on your own components is one of
the gaps worth taking on in the build block; see
[Controls, Policies & Ready-Made CRs](/controls-and-policies) for what the
perimeter enforces today.
:::

This command proves the whole module: your terminal reaches the cluster, the
tool passed review, and the gateway publishes its route.

```bash
kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"  "}{.status.endpoint}{"\n"}'
```

It prints `Approved` followed by the tool's endpoint.

Next: [Module 3: Platform Check](/prove-the-platform).

---
title: "Step 4: Get your gateway credential"
weight: 40
---

In this step you extract your team's gateway API key, then prove for yourself
that the gateway is the only way to a model in this account. At the end the
key is in `/tmp/modaas-token`, where every later probe reads it, and you have
tested the three controls that shut the other doors.

**Why a gateway credential at all.** Nothing in this account talks to a model
directly: not you, not your agents, not a pod in the cluster. Every model and
tool call enters through one door, the governed gateway `modaas-agw`. That is
what makes governance possible: the door is where the caller is identified,
where the policy decision (Cedar) is made, where the guardrail is applied, and
where the call is recorded with a trace id and token counts. A door is only a
door if the walls hold, so this step has two halves: first you get the key
that opens the door; then you test the three walls yourself (sections 2 to 4):
your own IAM role cannot call Bedrock, your pods carry no AWS identity, and
your pods cannot reach a model endpoint over the network. Every later module
builds on this: the agents you build are told the gateway address and this
credential, nothing else, and every piece of evidence you hand in was recorded
at this door.

The governed gateway, `modaas-agw`, admits a caller only with a credential.
Your team's key is stored in a Kubernetes secret in the gateway's namespace.
Copy it to a file only you can read:

```bash
kubectl -n agentgateway-system get secret agw-apikeys \
  -o jsonpath='{.data}' | python3 -c "
import sys, json, base64
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print(base64.b64decode(next(iter(d.values()))).decode())
" > /tmp/modaas-token
chmod 600 /tmp/modaas-token
wc -c < /tmp/modaas-token
```

The last line prints the file's size in bytes (49 on the capture event,
2026-09-29). Zero means the secret was not read; run
`kubectl -n agentgateway-system get secret agw-apikeys` to see why.

The gateway accepts two kinds of identity. This API key is the simplest and
is what every probe in this workshop uses. The other is a JWT issued by the
Canvas's identity service for one governed resource, so that resource calls
as itself. Either way the authorization gateway, `modaas-authz`, resolves who
you are first, and only then does the policy engine (Cedar) decide whether
that caller may use the model or tool. A call with no credential is refused
before it reaches any model; you see that refusal for yourself in
[Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough).

heading_path: 2. Prove you cannot call a model directly
chunks.text:
Try to call a model with the AWS CLI, around the gateway:

```bash
aws bedrock-runtime converse --model-id nvidia.nemotron-nano-9b-v2 \
  --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"hi"}]}]' 2>&1 | cut -c1-160
```

It is refused with `AccessDeniedException` (captured 2026-09-29). In the IDE
the message ends `because no identity-based policy allows the
bedrock:InvokeModel action`: the IDE's role has no `bedrock:InvokeModel`
permission. In CloudShell, as the participant role, it ends `with an explicit
deny in an identity-based policy`: your participant role is explicitly denied.

heading_path: 3. Prove your pods carry no AWS identity
chunks.text:
A pod gets AWS credentials only through an
[Amazon EKS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/what-is-eks.html)
Pod Identity association.
List them:

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
CLUSTER=$(aws eks list-clusters --region "$REGION" --query 'clusters[0]' --output text)
aws eks list-pod-identity-associations --cluster-name "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" \
  --query 'associations[].[namespace,serviceAccount]' --output text
```

Every association belongs to the platform (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
modaas-system   aws-model-operator
modaas-system   aws-agent-operator
kube-system     ebs-csi-controller-sa
agentgateway-system     modaas-agw
modaas-system   aws-tool-operator
modaas-system   modaas-otel-collector
```

heading_path: 3. Prove your pods carry no AWS identity
chunks.text:
None is in `components`, the namespace your work runs in, so nothing you
deploy there has an AWS credential to misuse. The gateway's own service
account, `modaas-agw`, holds the only Bedrock permission in the account that
can call a model. That permission covers every foundation model in three
Regions; what narrows it to your models is the gateway, which routes only the
models your ModelConfigs declare and asks Cedar who may call each one.

heading_path: 4. Prove your pods cannot reach a model endpoint
chunks.text:
A NetworkPolicy, `components-egress-governed-only`, limits where pods in
`components` can send traffic: DNS in `kube-system`, `canvas-system`,
`agentgateway-system`, istiod in `istio-system`, `modaas-system`, and other
pods in `components`. Try the Bedrock endpoint from a throwaway pod there:

```bash
kubectl run egress-probe -n components --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.5.0 -- \
  sh -c 'curl -sS -m 10 -o /dev/null https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com; echo "curl exit=$?"' >/dev/null
sleep 25; kubectl logs egress-probe -n components
kubectl delete pod egress-probe -n components --wait=false
```

The connection times out (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 10001 milliseconds
curl exit=28
```

Exit code 28 is curl's timeout: the packets are dropped, so from your
namespace the model endpoint does not exist.

```bash
test -s /tmp/modaas-token && echo "credential ready"
```

It prints `credential ready`.

Next: [Step 5: Learn the API surface](/platform-access/api-surface).

title: "Module 2: Platform Access"
weight: 22
---

In this module you open your IDE, confirm the platform finished installing,
connect to the cluster, pick up your gateway credential, and call your first
governed tool. At the end you have a working terminal with `kubectl` pointed
at your cluster, the credential every later probe uses, and proof that the
only way to a model in this account is through the governed gateway.

Your account comes with a browser-based IDE (Code Editor, built on VS Code)
running on its own EC2 instance. It already has the AWS CLI, `kubectl`,
`helm`, `git` and Python installed, a kubeconfig for your cluster, and the
the tools this workshop uses installed. You do every step of this workshop in
its terminal.

The module has seven short steps. Do them in order; each one uses what the
previous one set up.

| Step | What you do | What you have afterwards |
|---|---|---|
| 1. [Open your IDE](/platform-access/open-ide) | Open the IDE from the event page | A terminal in your account |
| 2. [Check the install finished](/platform-access/install-status) | Read the installer's status line | Confidence the platform is up |
| 3. [Connect to the cluster](/platform-access/cluster-access) | Refresh the kubeconfig and list the nodes | `kubectl` working |
| 4. [Get your gateway credential](/platform-access/gateway-credential) | Extract the team API key; prove the other doors are shut | `/tmp/modaas-token` |
| 5. [Learn the API surface](/platform-access/api-surface) | See where governed endpoints come from and the four surfaces you use | The quick reference for the event |
| 6. [Ask Amazon Q about AWS](/platform-access/amazon-q) | Open Amazon Q in the console | Help for AWS questions, and its limits |
| 7. [Call your first governed tool](/platform-access/docs-tool) | Deploy, approve and call the documentation tool | A search tool for the platform docs, and the module checkpoint |

Start with [Step 1: Open your IDE](/platform-access/open-ide).

---
title: "Step 2: Check the install finished"
weight: 20
---

In this step you confirm that the platform install inside your account has
finished. At the end you will know the platform is ready, or how long to
wait. Everything after this page assumes it has finished, so this one line
saves you from debugging a platform that is simply still starting.

When your account is created, the IDE instance runs an installer in the
background. It waits for the cluster, installs the ODA Canvas, installs the
governed gateway (agentgateway), builds the five MoDaaS images in your
account's own CodeBuild project, and installs the MoDaaS chart. It takes
10 to 15 minutes and writes one status line as it goes.

```bash
cat ~/.modaas-bootstrap/status
```

When the install is done you see `READY`, the finish time, and how long it
took (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
READY 2026-09-29T02:24:41Z (641s)
```

The line can read three ways:

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `READY <time> (<seconds>s)` | The platform is installed and verified | Continue |
| `RUNNING <n>/8 <step>` | Still installing; `<step>` says which of the eight steps | Wait. To watch it, run `tail -f ~/.modaas-bootstrap/bootstrap.log` and press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop watching |
| `FAILED <n>/8 <step>: <reason>` | A step failed | Tell a facilitator and quote the line. Re-running is safe and resumes where it stopped: `bash ~/.modaas-bootstrap/bootstrap-platform.sh` |

```bash
grep -q '^READY' ~/.modaas-bootstrap/status && echo "install finished" || cat ~/.modaas-bootstrap/status
```

It prints `install finished`. If it prints a `RUNNING` line instead, wait and
run it again; do not continue until it says `install finished`.

Next: [Step 3: Connect to the cluster](/platform-access/cluster-access).

---
title: "Step 1: Open your IDE"
weight: 10
---

In this step you open the browser IDE for your account and its terminal.
At the end you have a shell running inside your AWS account, with the tools
and credentials this workshop needs already in place.

You will do every step of this workshop from this terminal. It already has
the AWS command line, `kubectl` and the workshop's own helper scripts, and it
is already signed in to your account, so you never install or configure
anything on your laptop. The two dialogs the IDE shows on first open look like
problems and are not; this page tells you what they are so you do not lose
your first ten minutes to them.

Go back to the Workshop Studio event page (the tab where you joined the event)
and choose **Event outputs** in the left menu. The table lists values your
account's [AWS CloudFormation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html)
stacks produced. Two of them matter today:

| Output | What it is |
|---|---|
| **IdeUrl** | Your IDE. The link carries a token, so there is no separate sign-in. |
| **CockpitUrl** | The MoDaaS cockpit, a read-only dashboard of the platform. You use it from Module 5 on. It also carries your token. |

If the event page is not to hand, the same link comes from the stack itself.
Run this in CloudShell (the terminal icon in the AWS console's top toolbar):

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$REGION" \
  --query "Stacks[].Outputs[?OutputKey=='IdeUrl'].OutputValue" --output text
```

An empty result means the IDE stack is still being created, not that
something is broken; wait a minute and run it again.

Treat both links like passwords: anyone who has them can open your IDE or read
your cockpit. Do not paste them into chat or tickets.

heading_path: 2. Open the IDE and its terminal
chunks.text:
Open the **IdeUrl** link. The IDE opens in a new tab and may ask whether you
trust the authors of the files in the folder; choose **Yes, I trust the
authors**. A "Get Started with Code Editor" walkthrough tab opens on first
use; close it, you do not need it.

Open a terminal with **Terminal > New Terminal** in the menu (or press
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>\`</kbd>). The first time you paste into it, the browser
asks for permission to use the clipboard; choose **Allow**.

![The IDE with its terminal open](/static/images/setup/ide-terminal-status.png)

The file explorer on the left shows your workspace folder, `environment`. It
starts empty. The modules put your agents, tools and evidence here. The
platform itself is already installed in your cluster; you work with it through
`kubectl`, the gateway and the cockpit, and you never need its source code.

Check who the terminal runs as:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text
```

The output names the IDE instance's role (captured 2026-09-29; your account
id and suffixes differ):

```text
arn:aws:sts::<account>:assumed-role/a-02-code-editor-IdeInstanceRole-<suffix>/i-<instance-id>
```

That role is how the IDE reaches your cluster and your account's AWS APIs. It
has no permission to call a model directly; you prove that in Step 4.

:::expand{header="Fallback: use AWS CloudShell if the IDE will not open"}
Use this only if the IDE does not load and a facilitator cannot fix it.
CloudShell is the terminal icon in the AWS console's top toolbar. It has your
participant credentials already loaded, but it does not have `kubectl`, it
times out when idle, and a timeout clears every variable you set.

Install `kubectl` at the cluster's version and set the Region:

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
mkdir -p ~/bin
curl -fsSL "https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/amazon-eks/1.36.2/2026-07-05/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl" -o /tmp/kubectl
install -m 0755 /tmp/kubectl ~/bin/kubectl && rm -f /tmp/kubectl
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH
echo "Region: $REGION"
```

After every reconnect, re-create the variables later modules use with the
rehydrate script. `source` it; running it as `./rehydrate.sh` sets the
variables in a subshell that then exits:

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/scripts/rehydrate.sh" source=s3}' -o ~/rehydrate.sh
chmod +x ~/rehydrate.sh
source ~/rehydrate.sh
```

Run these in CloudShell, not on your laptop: the `kubectl` binary above is for
Linux, and a laptop has no workshop credentials. Then continue with Step 3.
Step 2 reads a file that exists only on the IDE instance, so skip it.
:::

```bash
kubectl version --client 2>&1 | head -1; helm version --short
```

Both tools answer with their versions: `kubectl` 1.36 and Helm 3.22 (captured
2026-09-29; the patch and build suffix are shown as `x`):

```text
Client Version: v1.36.x-eks-xxxxxxx
v3.22.0+g144ca65
```

Next: [Step 2: Check the install finished](/platform-access/install-status).

---
title: "The control plane: MoDaaS operators"
weight: 253
---

You will check the MoDaaS deployments and confirm the model operator is
watching its resource type. At the end you know the control plane is live,
not only installed.

```bash
kubectl get deploy -n modaas-system
```

Six deployments, all at their full replica count (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
NAME                      READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
aws-agent-operator        1/1     1            1           129m
aws-model-operator        1/1     1            1           129m
aws-tool-operator         1/1     1            1           129m
modaas-authz              2/2     2            2           129m
modaas-pdp                2/2     2            2           129m
opentelemetry-collector   1/1     1            1           129m
```

| Deployment | What it does |
|---|---|
| `aws-model-operator` | Reconciles `ModelConfig`: turns a declared model into a guardrail, a gateway route and a policy |
| `aws-tool-operator` | Reconciles `ToolConfig` |
| `aws-agent-operator` | Reconciles `AgentConfig` |
| `modaas-pdp` | The Cedar policy decision point: decides who may call what |
| `modaas-authz` | The authorization gateway: resolves who is calling, then asks the policy decision point |
| `opentelemetry-collector` | Collects telemetry from the platform |

Running is not the same as reconciling. An operator that cannot watch its
resource type says so as soon as it starts, so check its start line:

```bash
kubectl logs -n modaas-system deploy/aws-model-operator | grep -m1 'Operator started'
```

Captured 2026-09-29:

title: "The perimeter: the governed gateway"
weight: 254

You will check that the gateway is programmed, list its listeners, and
verify the policies that cover them. At the end you know there is one door
with two rooms behind it, not two perimeters that can drift apart.

The gateway `modaas-agw` is the only door to a model or tool. Check that it is
programmed and has an address:

```bash
kubectl get gateway modaas-agw -n agentgateway-system
```

`PROGRAMMED` reads `True` and `ADDRESS` is a load balancer host (captured
2026-09-29; your host differs):

```text
NAME         CLASS          ADDRESS      PROGRAMMED   AGE
modaas-agw   agentgateway   <elb-host>   True         131m
```

List its listeners, the ports it accepts traffic on:

```bash
kubectl get gateway modaas-agw -n agentgateway-system \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.listeners[*]}{.name}{" "}{.port}{" "}{.protocol}{"\n"}{end}'
```

Captured 2026-09-29:

```text
http 8080 HTTP
llm 8081 HTTP
llm-tls 8443 HTTPS
```

`llm` and `llm-tls` carry model calls (`/v1/chat/completions`); `http`
carries tool calls (`/mcp/<alias>`). Now check which policies apply to them:

```bash
kubectl get agentgatewaypolicy -n agentgateway-system \
  -o custom-columns='POLICY:.metadata.name,SECTIONS:.spec.targetRefs[*].sectionName,ACCEPTED:.status.ancestors[0].conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].status'
```

Four policies, all accepted (captured 2026-09-29):

```text
POLICY                 SECTIONS      ACCEPTED
modaas-access-log      <none>        True
modaas-authz           <none>        True
modaas-llm-auth        llm,llm-tls   True
modaas-mcp-ratelimit   http          True
```

`<none>` under `SECTIONS` means the policy targets the whole gateway, every
listener. So `modaas-authz`, the identity and Cedar authorization check,
covers model and tool traffic alike, and so does the access log. That is what
makes this one door with two rooms behind it, rather than two perimeters that
can drift apart. `modaas-llm-auth` adds the API-key check on the model
listeners, and `modaas-mcp-ratelimit` rate-limits tool calls.

```bash
kubectl get agentgatewaypolicy -n agentgateway-system --no-headers -o custom-columns=':.status.ancestors[0].conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].status' | grep -c True
```

It prints 4. All four gateway policies are accepted.

---
title: "Kill switch"
weight: 545
---

You will pause a tool and see the next agent call fail immediately. At the
end you know that pausing a governed resource removes its route and restores
it on unpause.

When a tool misbehaves in production you need every agent to stop reaching
it within seconds, without touching any agent. Because agents reach tools only
through the gateway, pausing the tool's declaration makes the platform remove
its route, and every caller fails closed at once. Judges ask about this
control first, and in Module 9 you run the same probe against your own
agent.

```bash
kubectl patch toolconfig modaas-docs -n components --type merge -p '{"spec":{"paused":true}}'
```

**Expected result:** the next call that reaches modaas-docs returns
tool initialize: HTTP 404: route not found. The gateway removed the route.

```bash
kubectl patch toolconfig modaas-docs -n components --type merge -p '{"spec":{"paused":false}}'
```

**Expected result:** the route returns within about 30 seconds and calls
succeed again. The same command works on a ModelConfig or an AgentConfig.

```bash
kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'
```

It prints Approved (not Paused).

You will run the fault-resolution scenario and read the evidence trail. At the

A governed system is one where you can reconstruct what happened after the
fact. This scenario makes three agents call models and tools in turn. Because
every one of those calls passed through the gateway, each record carries the
same correlation id, and following that id through the records is how you
prove, rather than assert, who called what, in what order, and what it cost.
Control 7 (event recording) is built on exactly this.

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/audit-store.py" source=s3}' -o /tmp/store.py
kubectl get secret audit-write-token -n components >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  kubectl create secret generic audit-write-token -n components \
    --from-literal=token="$(head -c16 /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')"
kubectl create configmap audit-store-app -n components \
  --from-file=store.py=/tmp/store.py --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/audit-store.yaml" source=s3}' | kubectl apply -f -
```

**Expected result:** the secret, ConfigMap, deployment and service are created.

heading_path: 2. Create a load-balanced address for runtimes
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/audit-store-agentcore.yaml" source=s3}' | kubectl apply -f -
until [ -n "$(kubectl get svc audit-store-agentcore -n components \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')" ]; do sleep 10; done
kubectl rollout status deploy/audit-store -n components --timeout=300s
```

**Expected result:** deployment "audit-store" successfully rolled out.

Download the Strands agent source the three reference agents share, then
build it in your account's CodeBuild project:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/reference-agent
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/reference-agent/agent.py" source=s3}' -o /tmp/reference-agent/agent.py
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/build-agent-image.sh" source=s3}' -o /tmp/bai.sh
TARGET=agentcore bash /tmp/bai.sh
```

**Expected result:** the build prints a digest reference (about 48 seconds).

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/reference-impl/make-agentcore-agents.py" source=s3}' \
  -o /tmp/make-agentcore-agents.py
python3 /tmp/make-agentcore-agents.py --region "$REGION"
kubectl apply -f /tmp/agents-agentcore.generated.yaml
for A in customer-experience-agent it-resolution-agent network-resolution-agent; do
  kubectl annotate agentconfig $A -n components \
    modaas.tmforum.org/approver="$(whoami)@team" \
    modaas.tmforum.org/approval-attestation="Reviewed: reference agent on AgentCore" --overwrite
done
for A in customer-experience-agent it-resolution-agent network-resolution-agent; do
  kubectl wait agentconfig/$A -n components \
    --for=condition=Provisioned --timeout=300s
done
```

**Expected result:** all three reach condition met (about 5 minutes total).

```bash
kubectl apply -f /tmp/agents-agentcore.generated.yaml
```

**Expected result:** network-resolution-agent configured, others unchanged.

title: "Swap the model, the governed way"
weight: 544
---

Swapping models is what MoDaaS is built for. You will change the IT agent
from nemotron-super-120b to nemotron-nano-9b and compare cost in the
evidence. At the end you have two runs to compare.

In a real network the model behind an agent changes for cost, latency or
vendor reasons, and today that usually means editing the agent and
redeploying it. Here the agent only knows a model alias; the platform maps the
alias to a real model behind the gateway. You change the mapping, the agent
code stays untouched, and the cost line in the records moves. This is the
clearest demonstration of why the governance layer sits between agent and
model.

The operator reprograms the runtime and the route. The agent code did not
change.

```bash
kubectl get modelconfig nemotron-nano-9b -n components \
  -o custom-columns='PHASE:.status.phase,ROUTE:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="AgentgatewayRouteProgrammed")].status'
```

**Expected result:** Approved and True.

```bash
kubectl patch agentconfig it-resolution-agent -n components --type=json -p '[
  {"op":"test",    "path":"/spec/dependsOn/models/0", "value":"nemotron-super-120b"},
  {"op":"replace", "path":"/spec/dependsOn/models/0", "value":"nemotron-nano-9b"},
  {"op":"replace", "path":"/spec/modelRef",            "value":"nemotron-nano-9b"}]'
```

**Expected result:** agentconfig patched.

Wait for the runtime to update:

```bash
GEN=$(kubectl get agentconfig it-resolution-agent -n components -o jsonpath='{.metadata.generation}')
kubectl wait agentconfig/it-resolution-agent -n components \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.observedGeneration}'="$GEN" --timeout=120s
```

**Expected result:** condition met (about 40 seconds).

heading_path: 3. Run the scenario again and compare
chunks.text:
```bash
bash /tmp/run-reference.sh
kubectl -n agentgateway-system logs deploy/modaas-agw --tail=200 \
  | grep 'listener=llm' | grep "it.resolution" | tail -2
```

**Expected result:** the earlier run shows
gen_ai.request.model=nvidia.nemotron-super-3-120b; the new run shows
nvidia.nemotron-nano-9b-v2 with different token counts.

```bash
kubectl -n components annotate agentconfig it-resolution-agent \
  modaas.tmforum.org/approval-attestation="Reviewed: model changed to nemotron-nano-9b for cost comparison" \
  --overwrite
```

**Expected result:** annotated.

```bash
kubectl get agentconfig it-resolution-agent -n components \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.modelRef}'
```

It prints nemotron-nano-9b.

title: "Glossary"
weight: 10
---

At the end of this page you can look up any platform term by name: what it
means here, what you do with it, and the module where it first appears.

| Term | What it is | What you do with it | First used |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[CR](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/)** (Custom Resource) | A Kubernetes object defined by a CRD. Every governed asset on this platform (model, tool, agent) is a CR. | `kubectl apply` to declare it, `kubectl get` to read it. | [Module 2](/platform-access) |
| **[CRD](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/)** (Custom Resource Definition) | The schema that defines a kind of CR. This platform adds four: ModelConfig, ToolConfig, AgentConfig, Registry. | `kubectl explain modelconfig` to read its fields. | [Module 4](/ai-native-oda-canvas) |
| **Operator** | A controller that watches CRs and reconciles them into running infrastructure. Three here: `aws-model-operator`, `aws-tool-operator`, `aws-agent-operator`. | You declare a CR; the operator does the work. | [Module 4](/ai-native-oda-canvas) |
| **Namespace** | A Kubernetes scope for names. Governed assets live in `components`; the gateway lives in `agentgateway-system`; platform internals live in `modaas-system`. | `kubectl get modelconfig -n components`. | [Module 2](/platform-access) |
| **`kubectl apply`** | Sends a CR to the API server. Admission validates it before storing. | Declare any governed asset. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **`kubectl annotate`** | Adds metadata to a resource. On this platform, the approval attestation is an annotation. | Approve a ModelConfig, ToolConfig or AgentConfig. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **`kubectl wait`** | Blocks until a condition or jsonpath matches on a resource. Safer than polling in a loop. | `kubectl wait modelconfig/nemotron-nano-9b -n components --for=condition=AgentgatewayRouteProgrammed`. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **Phase** | The `.status.phase` field on a governed CR: `Reviewing`, `Approved`, `Paused`, `Revoking`. The single authority for whether a resource is live. | Read it with `kubectl get modelconfig -n components -o custom-columns='PHASE:.status.phase'`. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |

| **Condition** | A `.status.conditions[]` entry recording one step of the operator's work (for example `AgentgatewayRouteProgrammed`). Conditions settle after the phase and can lag. | Read them to debug a stuck resource. Phase is authoritative, not conditions. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **[ModelConfig](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/model-as-a-service-crds)** | A CR declaring a governed model: the Bedrock model id, the guardrail, and which callers may use it. | Declare, approve, and the operator creates a guardrail and a gateway route. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **[ToolConfig](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/model-as-a-service-crds)** | A CR declaring a governed tool. Provider `agentCoreGateway` means a Lambda target on the account's AgentCore Gateway. | Declare and approve. The gateway exposes it at `/mcp/<alias>`. | [Module 2](/platform-access/docs-tool) |
| **[AgentConfig](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/model-as-a-service-crds)** | A CR declaring a governed agent: its image, its model and tool dependencies, and its safety posture. | Declare, approve, and the operator creates an AgentCore Runtime. | [Module 7](/reference-agents) |
| **Registry record** | An entry in [AWS Agent Registry](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry.html) for a governed asset. Created by the operator on approval. | Read `status.registryRecordId` on any approved CR. | [Module 7](/reference-agents) |
| **Attestation** | The human approval statement recorded as annotations on a CR: who approved, and what they checked. | `kubectl annotate ... modaas.tmforum.org/approver=... modaas.tmforum.org/approval-attestation=...`. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **[Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com/) policy** | A policy document loaded by the PDP. Each approved model gets a Cedar permit naming its declared consumers. | Author policy in a ConfigMap; the operator loads it. | [Module 6](/controls-and-policies) |
| **Guardrail** | An [Amazon Bedrock Guardrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html) the operator creates from the ModelConfig's safety declaration. Sits in the gateway's call path. | Declared on the ModelConfig; enforced by Bedrock. You do not create it yourself. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |

| **Run id** | The gateway's name for a single scenario execution. Equals the `traceparent` trace id when every call in the run sends one. | Sum tokens per run with `grep 'modaas.run_id="<id>"'` on the gateway log. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **Correlation id (CID)** | The scenario run's own id, minted by `run-reference.sh` or `ask-agent.sh`. Exported as `$CID`. | Pass to the evidence ledger and scoring tools: `score-run.py $CID`. | [Module 7](/reference-agents) |
| **`traceparent`** | The [W3C trace-context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) header sent by callers. Becomes `modaas.trace_id` on the gateway line and the trace id in spans. | Send it on every call so one run stays one trace. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |
| **Evidence ledger** | The `audit-store` service in `components`. Agents append records (intent, invocation, result-inspection) per phase of work. Gated by a write token. | Read a run: `kubectl get --raw ".../proxy/timeline?cid=$CID"`. | [Module 7](/reference-agents) |
| **Trace** | A set of spans sharing one trace id, collected from AgentCore runtimes into per-runtime [CloudWatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch.html) log groups. | `python3 /tmp/show-run-spans.py <trace_id>`. | [Module 8](/agent-observability) |
| **Log group** | A [CloudWatch Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Working-with-log-groups-and-streams.html) group. The gateway writes to `/aws/modaas/gateway`; each AgentCore runtime writes to `/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/<id>-DEFAULT`. | `kubectl logs` for the gateway; `aws logs` for AgentCore spans. | [Module 8](/agent-observability) |
| **[AgentCore Runtime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agents-tools-runtime.html)** | The AWS service that hosts your agent container. The operator creates one per approved AgentConfig. Runs `linux/arm64` only. | The operator manages it. You build the image; AgentCore runs it. | [Module 7](/reference-agents) |

| **[AgentCore Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway.html)** | An AWS service that fronts Lambda tool targets with IAM auth. ToolConfigs with provider `agentCoreGateway` point at a Lambda behind this gateway. | Declare a ToolConfig with provider `agentCoreGateway` and a Lambda ARN. | [Module 2](/platform-access/docs-tool) |
| **Lambda tool** | An [AWS Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html) function registered as a target on the account's AgentCore Gateway. Gateway Lambda tools are the default tool provider. | Declared via ToolConfig with `provider: agentCoreGateway`. | [Module 2](/platform-access/docs-tool) |
| **IDE role** | The IAM role assumed by your browser IDE instance. It can read the cluster and call the AWS CLI, but cannot invoke Bedrock models directly. | Every `kubectl` and `aws` command in the IDE runs as this role. | [Module 2](/platform-access) |
| **Cockpit** | A read-only web UI over the governed estate: governance pipeline, traces, cost, graph view. Already running at `CockpitUrl`. | Open from Event outputs. Read the Trace and Cost views after any run. | [Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) |

```bash
kubectl api-resources --api-group=oda.tmforum.org --no-headers -o custom-columns='KIND:.kind'
```

It lists `AgentConfig`, `ModelConfig`, `ToolConfig` and any other CRDs the
platform registers: every kind this glossary names.

ServiceNow's guide to its own documentation is on the next page,
[ServiceNow documentation set](/resources/servicenow-docs). When you are ready
to tear down, go to [Cleanup](/cleanup).
