The map legend for your build. Nothing here is required reading, come back
when you need it.

:::alert{type="info" header="What good looks like"}
The cockpit is read-only over the same APIs you use from the CLI, everything it shows, `kubectl` and `curl` can show too. Use it to *verify*, not to *act*.
:::

The Graph view, the governed path, drawn from live telemetry. Edge thickness
and motion come from the gateway's own OpenTelemetry counters, so an idle
platform draws thin, still edges and a busy one does not:

![Graph view, three agents converging on the single governed gateway, then out to models and tools, with edge weight from live request counts](/static/images/ui-graph-view.png)

Read the thin gray edge as carefully as the thick ones: `demo-crm-lookup` is
**declared but never exercised**. A governed asset nobody calls is exactly the
kind of thing an auditor asks about, and the graph surfaces it without being
asked.

The Governance view, every governed asset, its phase, and the full pipeline each one walked:

![Governance view, 7 governed assets, all Approved, with the Declare → Revoke pipeline](/static/images/ui-governance-view.png)

The Observability view, the gateway's own OpenTelemetry GenAI metrics, per model:

![Observability view, token consumption, latency, and traffic per governed route](/static/images/ui-observability-view.png)

`ask-agent.sh <agent> "<question>"` is the single invocation path for any
governed agent. It resolves the region and runtime ARN from the AgentConfig
status, mints a correlation id, sends `traceparent` and baggage
`modaas-correlation-id=<CID>`, and prints the answer. Underneath it calls
`ask_agent.py`, which makes this API call:

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
ARN=$(kubectl get agentconfig my-agent -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.agentRuntimeArn}')
CID="my-agent-$(date +%s)-$(od -An -N3 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"
printf '{"correlation_id":"%s","context":{"question":"How does a ModelConfig get approved?"}}' "$CID" > /tmp/ask.json
aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-agent-runtime --region "$REGION" --agent-runtime-arn "$ARN" \
  --runtime-session-id "$CID-$(python3 -c 'import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4().hex)')" \
  --content-type application/json --accept application/json \
  --payload fileb:///tmp/ask.json /tmp/answer.json >/dev/null && cat /tmp/answer.json; echo
```

Use `ask-agent.sh` instead of this block: it handles traceparent, baggage,
and exports `$CID` for you.

heading_path: Your terminal lost its variables: get them back
chunks.text:
A new IDE terminal tab, a reloaded IDE page, or the CloudShell fallback after
an idle timeout all start without the variables earlier pages exported:
`REGION`, `STACK_NAME`, `ECR_HOST`, `MODAAS_SHA` and `NODE_ROLE_ARN` are empty.

An empty variable rarely announces itself. `REGION` falls back to a default
rather than failing, and an empty `ECR_HOST` produces an image reference like
`/my-repo@sha256:…` that only fails later, at pull time, a long way from the
cause. If a command that worked ten minutes ago now behaves strangely, check
this first:

```bash
source ~/rehydrate.sh
```

If you do not have it yet:

```bash
curl -sSL ':assetUrl{path="/scripts/rehydrate.sh" source=s3}' -o ~/rehydrate.sh
source ~/rehydrate.sh
```

`source` it rather than executing it, exports do not survive a subshell. It
derives everything from your cluster and its
[CloudFormation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html)
stack, is read-only,
and is safe to run as often as you like. It prints what it resolved and ends with
`kubectl get nodes`.

A pending digest is normal until CodeBuild has pushed the image.

Each row is a symptom seen on a workshop account on 2026-09-28 or 2026-09-29,
its cause, and the fix.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The IDE or cockpit page answers `403` | The link lost its `?tkn=` token | Reopen **IdeUrl** or **CockpitUrl** from **Event outputs**; do not retype it ([Module 2, Step 1](/platform-access/open-ide)) |
| A model call answers `404 route not found` | The ModelConfig is not approved yet, its route is still being programmed, or it is paused | Check `kubectl get modelconfig <alias> -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.phase} {.spec.paused}'`; after approval wait for the route ([Module 5](/baseline-walkthrough) section 2); after an unpause allow about a minute ([Module 6](/controls-and-policies) section 3) |
| A call through the gateway is refused with `401` or `403` | Missing or wrong gateway key, or a Cedar policy denies this caller or asset | Re-read the key from `/tmp/modaas-token` ([Module 2, Step 4](/platform-access/gateway-credential)); an unapproved model is refused exactly like an undeclared one |
| `kubectl apply` says `safety.required=true cannot be combined with enforcer.kind=none` | Admission refuses a model that requires a guardrail but names no enforcer | Name the enforcer (`bedrockGuardrail`) or set `required: false` ([Module 4, Step 1](/ai-native-oda-canvas/what-modaas-does)) |
| A resource stays in `Reviewing` | Nobody has attested to it: the approval annotation is missing or misspelled | Re-run the `kubectl annotate ... modaas.tmforum.org/approver=...` command from the page you are on |
| Invoking your agent says `An error occurred when starting the runtime` | The container fails at start (on 2026-09-29: an unpinned package changed an import) | Read the runtime's log: `aws logs describe-log-streams --log-group-name /aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/<runtime-id>-DEFAULT`, then the newest stream; pin the package and rebuild ([Module 9, Step 2](/build-your-own-agent/what-the-script-did)) |
| `docker push` to [Amazon ECR](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/what-is-ecr.html) is refused | Only the CodeBuild image-build role may push | Build through `build-agent-image.sh` or `new-agent.sh` ([Module 9](/build-your-own-agent)) |

heading_path: Evidence tour: where each auditor answer lives
chunks.text:
| Auditor question | Surface | Starting point |
|------------------|---------|----------------|
| WHO acted | gateway identity records | authz service logs: `kubectl logs -n modaas-system deploy/modaas-authz` |
| WHAT was touched | programmed routes + CR events | `kubectl get agentgatewaymodel -A` · `kubectl get events -n components` |
| WAS IT AUTHORIZED | Cedar PDP decisions | `kubectl logs -n modaas-system deploy/modaas-pdp` |
| WHO APPROVED | attestation annotations | the jsonpath from [Baseline Walkthrough](/baseline-walkthrough) section 7, "Read who approved it" |
| INTEGRITY | CloudTrail + Kubernetes audit | `aws cloudtrail lookup-events --max-results 10` |
| RECONSTRUCT | the evidence log group and the decision log, joined on `action_id` | `aws logs tail /modaas/evidence --since 1h` · the PDP log line with the same `action_id` ([Module 6](/controls-and-policies), Observability) |

Every asset follows the same lifecycle: declare → admission validation →
approval attestation → Approved → serving.

1. Write the CR (start from the demo: `kubectl get modelconfig nemotron-nano-9b -n components -o yaml`).
2. Apply it. Admission (CEL) rejects self-contradictory governance up front.
3. Record the approval attestation (Baseline Walkthrough section 2, "Approve one model").
4. Poll bounded, never `kubectl get -w`. Replace `<your-alias>` with your
   ModelConfig name (`kubectl get modelconfig -n components` lists the valid names):

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  PHASE=$(kubectl get modelconfig <your-alias> -n components \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}')
  echo "phase=$PHASE"
  [ "$PHASE" = "Approved" ] && break
  sleep 10
done
```

Moved to its own page: [Controls, Policies & Ready-Made CRs](/controls-and-policies) , 
guardrails, runtime Cedar policies, observability, and the catalog of
ready-made governed-asset declarations.

heading_path: Ask the docs: the governed knowledge base
chunks.text:
`modaas-docs` is a `ToolConfig`: the ODA Canvas and MoDaaS documentation
behind the gateway's MCP listener, so "which field is that" and "why is it
shaped this way" become a tool call rather than a tab hunt. It is not
pre-installed. You deploy and approve it yourself in
[Platform Access, Step 7](/platform-access/docs-tool), as the first governed tool you
touch. This section covers what is in it and how to reach it afterwards.

heading_path: Ask the docs: the governed knowledge base
chunks.text:
| | |
|---|---|
| In-cluster URL | `http://modaas-agw.agentgateway-system:8080/mcp/modaas-docs`, bearer `$(cat /tmp/modaas-token)` |
| Published URL | `kubectl get toolconfig modaas-docs -n components -o jsonpath='{.status.endpoint}'`: the same route on the gateway's public load balancer. That listener is plain HTTP, so the bearer token would cross the internet unencrypted. Call it from inside the cluster |
| Protocol | MCP over streamable HTTP: `initialize` first, then every request carries the `Mcp-Session-Id` the server returned |
| Tools | `search_docs(query, limit?, source?)` · `get_doc(id)` |
| Every response carries | `source_path` and `heading_path`: no answer without a citation |
| Corpus | public sources only, each at a pinned commit: TM Forum `oda-canvas` design docs and operator READMEs (`oda-canvas`) · the TM Forum AI-native canvas decision log (`ai-canvas`) · the published MoDaaS CRDs (`modaas`) · this workshop's own module pages (`workshop`) |
| Retrieval | BM25 over a shipped index. No embeddings, no model call: it answers while Bedrock is throttled and never adds to your spend |
| Backend | `deploy/modaas-docs-mcp` in `components`, a ClusterIP Service with the index mounted from ConfigMaps |
| Health | `kubectl exec deploy/modaas-docs-mcp -n components -- python3 -c "import urllib.request;print(urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8080/healthz').read().decode())"` |

heading_path: Ask the docs: the governed knowledge base
chunks.text:
To give your own agent the tool, declare the dependency so the composition
gate checks it is `Approved` before your agent is:

```yaml
  dependsOn:
    models: ["nemotron-nano-9b"]
    tools: ["modaas-docs"]
```

Then connect with an MCP client that sends the bearer token. With Strands:

```python
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient

docs = MCPClient(lambda: streamablehttp_client(
    "http://modaas-agw.agentgateway-system:8080/mcp/modaas-docs",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}))
```

`api_key` is the `GATEWAY_API_KEY` your AgentConfig already mounts from
`agw-apikeys` in [Module 9](/build-your-own-agent). The client handles the
`initialize` handshake and the session header. A bare HTTP POST of
`tools/call` does not, and the gateway refuses it with
`mcp: session header is required for non-initialize requests`. An agent that
cites `source_path` in its output is showing an auditor a chain it can follow,
which is the bar the challenge scores.

heading_path: Ask the docs: the governed knowledge base
chunks.text:
If a query returns nothing useful, try the field or kind name verbatim
(`ModelConfig`, `dataClassification`, `ExposedAPI`). Retrieval is
keyword-based, so an exact identifier beats a paraphrase. The corpus is built
from an allow-list, and the builder refuses any file that names a customer, so
a few MoDaaS design docs are absent by design.

The MoDaaS documentation site is not hosted in this environment. The MoDaaS
design documents are not published either. What you can read is public: the
CRDs in
[`model-as-a-service-crds`](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/model-as-a-service-crds),
the architecture decisions in
[`ai-canvas-architecture`](https://github.com/tmforum-oda/ai-canvas-architecture),
and, for the schema your cluster actually runs, `kubectl explain` on any of the
four kinds. `modaas-docs` serves the public documents: `search_docs` finds the
passage, and `get_doc` with a bare `source_path` (for example
`ai-canvas/decision-log/ADR-004-gateway-mediation-architecture.md`) returns the
whole document reassembled in order.

A live, read-only view of the governed estate. Use it to check your work, or
as a starting point (or a counterexample) for your own evidence presentation.

**It is already running.** Provisioning starts it for your team as the
`modaas-cockpit` service on the IDE instance. There is nothing to install or
launch, and it runs in the cloud, so any browser reaches it.

Find its URL on your event page in Workshop Studio: open the **Event outputs**
table and read the **CockpitUrl** row. Open it from there rather than typing
or retyping it, the same way you opened **IdeUrl** in
[Module 2](/platform-access). If you need it from a terminal instead, ask
CloudFormation directly from CloudShell or the IDE terminal for the same
value:

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$REGION" \
  --query "Stacks[].Outputs[?OutputKey=='CockpitUrl'].OutputValue" --output text
```

:::alert{header="If the page does not load yet" type="info"}
The cockpit installs its Python dependencies on first boot and restarts until
healthy, so it can trail the rest of your environment by a minute or two.
Refresh once; it needs nothing from you.
:::

The cockpit has its own [Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html)
distribution, separate from the IDE's. Your browser talks HTTPS to CloudFront.
CloudFront talks plain HTTP to the IDE instance on port 8081, where nginx
passes the request to the UI server on `127.0.0.1:9000`. The instance's
security group admits port 8081 only from CloudFront's origin-facing address
range, so there is no path to the UI that skips CloudFront. It has a
distribution of its own because the UI calls absolute `/api/...` paths, which
under the IDE's distribution would land on the code editor instead.

:::alert{type="warning" header="The URL is the key: treat it like a password"}
The `CockpitUrl` ends in `?tkn=` and your environment's access token, the same
token your IDE URL carries. nginx on the IDE instance swaps it for a cookie on
the first request and answers `403 Forbidden` to any request that has neither.
Anyone who has the full URL can read everything the cockpit shows: every
governed CR in full, their approvers, your account ID and cluster name, and
gateway traffic. It cannot change anything, because every route the server
exposes is a read (HTTP GET). It reads the cluster as the IDE instance's role,
the same identity as your IDE terminal. Keep the URL out of shared channels and
out of screenshots that show the address bar.
:::

15 views, left nav. Each view has its own hash route, so you can open one
directly: append `#governance`, `#trace` and so on to the `CockpitUrl`. A
path such as `/governance` returns `404`. An unknown hash opens Overview. The
list is:

| View | What it answers |
|---|---|
| **Graph** | The one-door topology: your agents → gateway → models/tools, edge width from real traffic. A thin gray edge is an asset declared but never exercised, the most auditor-relevant thing on screen. |
| **Composition** | Is every dependency attested? |
| **Dependencies** | What composes with what. |
| **Overview** | Is the platform healthy? It opens on which cluster the console is reading, and whether the zone NetworkPolicies are enforced. |
| **Governance** | What is approved, and prove it: every governed asset with its phase, and the Declare → Admit → Approve → Authorize → Enforce → Attest → Revoke pipeline with live counts. Select a row for the live CR: conditions, Kubernetes events and the full YAML. |
| **Relationships** | How coupled is the platform? |
| **Trace** | One invocation, end to end: sequence lifelines, the agent-to-model/tool pipeline, and a replay control that lights each hop in order. It reads traces from [AWS X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray.html), and the gateway in this build has no tracing configured, so it reports *No governed trace recorded yet*. Until then, reconstruct a call from the audit store timeline ([Reference agents](/reference-agents)) and the `modaas-authz` log. |
| **Perimeter** | What the gateway is enforcing, read from agentgateway's admin port. This deployment does not expose that port, so the view opens on *The gateway is not publishing its config* (the admin surface is not listening on `:15000`). The same facts from the CLI: `kubectl get agentgatewaypolicies -A`. |
| **Canvas** | How assets compose as ODA Canvas components (TMF view). |
| **Infrastructure** | What the Canvas operator built. |
| **Runtime** | What is actually running vs what is declared. |
| **Observability** | Tokens, latency, and traffic per governed call, from the gateway's own OpenTelemetry GenAI metrics. |
| **Cost** | Per-model token spend and its USD cost, priced from the gateway's own price catalog, with a window selector (24h/7d). A model with no price in the catalog shows `has_pricing=false` and the reason, rather than a silent `$0`. |
| **Catalog** | What others can discover about your assets. |

Start in **Governance** after applying your first CR: watching your asset walk
the pipeline to `Approved` is the fastest way to see what the platform does.
For the lifecycle history behind it, the platform's own notification ledger is
one command away:

```bash
kubectl get publishednotifications -n components --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp \
  -o custom-columns='TIME:.metadata.creationTimestamp,EVENT:.spec.eventType,KIND:.spec.sourceRef.kind,ASSET:.spec.sourceRef.name'
```

**Facilitators:** the unit is `modaas-cockpit` on the IDE instance. Its
startup verdict is in `/var/log/modaas-cockpit-health.txt` and in the
[Amazon CloudWatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch.html) metric `MoDaaS/Workshop` `CockpitUnitHealthy` (dimension
`StackName`), so you can check it without a shell on the instance.

This page has no checkpoint of its own: it is reference material you return to
from any module. For a quick lookup of any platform term, see the
[Glossary](/resources/glossary). For ServiceNow's own guide to its AI agent,
security and AI Control Tower documentation, see the
[ServiceNow documentation set](/resources/servicenow-docs).

ServiceNow prepared this guide to its public product documentation for the
hackathon (August 2026). It is reproduced here unchanged
so you can bookmark it and work from it during the event. Use it with
[Module 11](/servicenow-integration), which shows how AI Control Tower sees the
assets you govern on this platform, and with
[Module 9](/build-your-own-agent) if your team also builds an agent on the
ServiceNow side.

Three documentation sets, one platform. Everything here comes from the public ServiceNow product documentation portal, so you can share it, bookmark it, and work from it during the hackathon.

Set one covers how to build an AI agent. Set two covers what that agent is allowed to see and do. Set three covers how you govern the whole portfolio once you have more than one. Start with set one if you are building. Read set two before you connect an agent to anything that writes.

All links point to the Australia release of the Enable AI documentation. Use the release selector at the top of any documentation page to switch to a different version.

title: "Module 11: ServiceNow AI Control Tower"
weight: 64
---

At the end of this module you can run a CloudTrail check that proves
ServiceNow AI Control Tower (AICT) acted in your account, explain what AICT
discovers about your governed assets and what it cannot see, and describe how
a connector identity reaches your account without you handling a key.

This module takes about 20 minutes. You need a terminal in your IDE and the
stack outputs from your event account. You do not need a ServiceNow instance
for the participant steps; the facilitator connects the instance if one is
available.

:::alert{type="info" header="ServiceNow documentation"}
Two ServiceNow docs anchor this module; open them alongside it:

- [AI Control Tower (AICT)](https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/intelligent-experiences/aict-landing.html)
- [AI Agent Studio (AIAS)](https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/intelligent-experiences/aias-landing.html)
- [ServiceNow documentation set for this hackathon](/resources/servicenow-docs): ServiceNow's own guide to the public docs, organized as build an agent, secure it, govern the portfolio

ServiceNow also provided three step-by-step guides for this hackathon
(PDF, download from the workshop assets):

| Guide | What it walks through |
|---|---|
| [Creating and Verifying Amazon Connection Setup](:assetUrl{path="/servicenow/creating-and-verifying-amazon-connection-setup.pdf" source=s3}) (12 pages) | Connecting AICT to an AWS account and confirming the connection |
| [AI Control Tower console: discovered assets and AI agents](:assetUrl{path="/servicenow/navigate-ai-control-tower-and-manage-ai-agents.pdf" source=s3}) (30 pages) | The AICT console: discovered assets, lifecycle, reviews |
| [Create and Manage AI Agents in ServiceNow AI Agent Studio](:assetUrl{path="/servicenow/create-and-manage-ai-agents-in-ai-agent-studio.pdf" source=s3}) (86 pages) | Building and managing agents in AI Agent Studio |
:::

:::alert{type="warning" header="What this build has run, and what it has not"}
The MoDaaS side runs on your event account. The
calls into a live ServiceNow instance have been run once, on a real
AWS-ServiceNow connection; AICT claims below come from that test, redacted.
If your event has no ServiceNow instance, steps 4 and 5 are described, not
exercised.
:::

The ServiceNow connector stack creates the IAM role and stores the connector
secret. Read its outputs from the IDE terminal:

```bash
export REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
STACK=$(aws cloudformation list-stacks --region "$REGION" \
  --stack-status-filter CREATE_COMPLETE UPDATE_COMPLETE \
  --query "StackSummaries[?ends_with(StackName,'servicenow-aict')].StackName | [0]" \
  --output text)
if [ -z "$STACK" ] || [ "$STACK" = "None" ]; then
  echo "AictConfigured false (no ServiceNow stack in this account; this is the default)"
else
  aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$REGION" --stack-name "$STACK" \
    --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[].[OutputKey,OutputValue]' --output table
fi
```

**Expected result:** if the stack is deployed, you see `AictConfigured true`,
`ServiceNowAictRoleName`, `ServiceNowAictSecretArn` and
`ServiceNowAictAccountId`. If the stack is not deployed, you see
`AictConfigured false`; the remaining steps still apply as described.

heading_path: 2. Fetch the connector secret and verify its role
chunks.text:
The connector's access key is stored in Secrets Manager. Your participant
role can read the secret value:

```bash
if [ -z "$STACK" ] || [ "$STACK" = "None" ]; then
  echo "No ServiceNow stack deployed; skipping secret fetch"
else
  SECRET_ARN=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$REGION" --stack-name "$STACK" \
    --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='ServiceNowAictSecretArn'].OutputValue" --output text)
  aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id "$SECRET_ARN" --region "$REGION" \
    --query SecretString --output text | python3 -m json.tool
fi
```

**Expected result:** if the stack is deployed, a JSON object with `AccessKeyId`
and `SecretAccessKey`. The key belongs to the connector IAM user, not to you.
If the stack is not deployed, you see the skip message.

:::alert{type="warning" header="Where this key goes"}
The key goes from this secret into the AICT connector form only. It is never
written to a file, never committed, and never shared. Stack deletion at the
end of the event removes the IAM user and the key.
:::

:::alert{type="info" header="Facilitator step"}
Then confirm the role the connector assumes (facilitator role required):

heading_path: 2. Fetch the connector secret and verify its role
chunks.text:
```bash
aws iam get-role --role-name SgcAictReadOnlyAccessRole \
  --query 'Role.{RoleName:RoleName,TrustPolicy:AssumeRolePolicyDocument}' --output json
```

**Expected result:** the role exists and its trust policy names exactly one
principal: the connector IAM user. The role grants read-only access to
AgentCore, Bedrock and CloudWatch Logs.
:::

A facilitator enters the redacted values below into the ServiceNow AI Service
Graph Connector for Amazon form. Participants do not enter these values.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Access key ID | `AKIA...` (from the secret in section 2) |
| Secret access key | (from the secret in section 2) |
| AWS regions | `us-east-1` |
| Target account IDs | your event account id |
| STS assume role | `SgcAictReadOnlyAccessRole` (role name only; the form prepends the ARN prefix) |

The guide "Creating and Verifying Amazon Connection Setup" above walks
through each field, including the CloudWatch log group for invocation counting.

After the facilitator connects the account, AICT discovers your AgentCore
runtimes, Bedrock agents and SageMaker models. It does not discover:

- Agents running as Kubernetes pods (no connector, no API for EKS)
- MCP servers (registered manually or from the MCP Catalog, not discovered)
- MoDaaS guardrails (the connector role lacks `bedrock:ListGuardrails`)
- Which ModelConfig served a call (all calls arrive under the gateway's
  single IAM principal)

Prove that AICT's own identity made the discovery calls in your account. Run
this from the IDE terminal:

```bash
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AssumeRole \
  --max-results 20 --region "$REGION" \
  --query 'Events[].CloudTrailEvent' --output json \
  | python3 -c "
import sys, json
for evt in json.load(sys.stdin):
    parsed = json.loads(evt)
    rp = parsed.get('requestParameters', {})
    role = rp.get('roleArn', '')
    if 'SgcAict' in role:
        print(f'caller={parsed[\"userIdentity\"][\"userName\"]} role={role.split(\"/\")[-1]} session={rp.get(\"roleSessionName\",\"\")}')
"
```

**Expected result:** one or more lines showing the connector user assuming
`SgcAictReadOnlyAccessRole`. The session name identifies the AICT discovery
run. If no lines appear, either the facilitator has not connected the
account yet or the CloudTrail events have not arrived (allow about 2 minutes).

When an agent chooses `escalate` (scenario S3 in
[Module 7](/reference-agents)), the refusal should open a ticket a human
already works, not a log line nobody reads. Rail 1 in the ServiceNow
integration creates an incident from the evidence chain.
[Module 7](/reference-agents) section 6 shows the `escalate` disposition.
Wiring it into your own agent's escalation path is a stretch goal for your
entry; `escalate-to-incident.py` in the workshop assets is the starting point.

```bash
aws iam get-role --role-name SgcAictReadOnlyAccessRole --query Role.RoleName --output text 2>/dev/null \
  && echo "role exists" || echo "no role (stack not deployed)"
```

It prints `role exists` if the ServiceNow stack was deployed, or `no role`
if the event does not use ServiceNow. Both are correct states.

If you are choosing which model to run your agent on next, go to
[Reference: Choosing a Model](/choosing-a-model).

title: "Getting Started"
weight: 10
---

This page tells you what your team is here to do, how the day and a half is
laid out, what you need to know beforehand, and the two rules that protect
your event. When you finish it you are ready to join the event and get into
your AWS account.

One telco customer outage flows through governed AI agents. Your team
operates, hardens and defends that flow across three escalating alert levels,
and wins by proving what happened.

The judging principle: *identify, protect and govern the scenarios. The
winner provides the strongest evidence that every decision is explainable,
every risk is controlled, and every claim can be independently verified.* In
practice the most auditable solution wins. Judges act as auditors and answer
six questions using only your evidence; the questions are in
[The Challenge](/challenge-brief).

An **audit-trail utility on top of the AI-native ODA Canvas**, plugged into
the platform's standard surfaces: the TMF639 resource inventory, the status
of each governed resource, attestations and the gateway's records. Every team
has the same access; nothing is privileged.

Your utility makes one management claim checkable: that the collaborating
agents meet the declared requirements for event recording, drift and token
spend. Build at least one of these three controls end to end:

- **Control 7, event recording:** every agent action lands in a record you
  can retrieve by run.
- **Control 9, drift:** you detect when behavior departs from a frozen
  baseline.
- **Control 16, token spend cap:** each run stays under a per-run token
  budget. This is the organizers' key ask.

One control done end to end is the floor. The Challenge page maps each
control to what to bring to judging.

| Block | What happens |
|-------|-------------|
| Orientation (1h) | Join the event, open your IDE, check the platform, tour it |
| Alert level 0, baseline (3h) | Run the flow end to end and capture your evidence baseline |
| Build block (3h) | Build your audit utility and safeguards |
| Alert level 1, hostile (4h) | Delays, tampered prompts, conflicting context: detect and degrade safely |
| Alert level 2, rogue (3h) | Bypass attempts, unauthorized actions, tampered records: contain and preserve |
| Reconstruction and judging (4h) | Generate your Evidence Pack; 15 minutes live with the judges |

- Basic Kubernetes (`kubectl apply`, `kubectl get`) and one programming
  language.
- AI or agent experience helps but is not required. The platform does the
  governing; you do the proving.
- A laptop with a current Chrome, Firefox or Edge. Everything else runs in
  the browser.
- Your team's **event access code**, which your event operator hands out.

heading_path: Two rules that protect your event
chunks.text:
:::alert{type="warning" header="1. Your account has a model-call ceiling: 100 requests a minute, 2.5 million tokens an hour"}
Every model call in your account passes through the governed gateway, and the
gateway enforces a per-account ceiling: **100 model requests per minute** and
**2.5 million tokens per hour**, across everything your team runs. Above the
ceiling the gateway answers `429 Too Many Requests` and the call is not made;
the model is never reached, so nothing is charged, but your agent sees an
error and your run stops.

Why it exists: the most common failure at a generative AI hackathon is a code
loop that hammers the model, and every team in the event draws on the same
Bedrock capacity. One request per second per agent (a short `sleep` in any
loop that calls the gateway) keeps a team comfortably under the ceiling. You
can watch your own usage against it in the cockpit's **Usage and cost** view,
and the ceiling itself is a governed policy you read in
[Module 6](/controls-and-policies).
:::

heading_path: Two rules that protect your event
chunks.text:
:::alert{type="warning" header="2. Back up your work as you go"}
Your account is destroyed when the event ends and cannot be recovered
afterwards. Push code to your own git repository as you go, and keep
infrastructure as YAML you can re-apply.
:::

`hackathon-helper` is a governed agent running on the same platform you use.
It explains MoDaaS concepts, reads your cluster state, writes CRs you apply
yourself, checks your evidence by run id, and answers AWS questions with
sources. It never applies, approves or changes anything.

Two ways to reach it; both go through the same governed path (gateway,
policy decision, evidence record), so a question is also a first governed
call you can later find in the trace view.

**From the IDE terminal.** `ask-agent.sh` is on the PATH of your IDE. It
prints the answer and a correlation id, and exports it as `$CID` so the
evidence commands in later modules pick it up:

```bash
ask-agent.sh hackathon-helper "How does a ModelConfig get approved?"
```

![The IDE terminal: ask-agent.sh returns the helper's answer with its source and a correlation id](/static/images/helper/ide-ask-agent.png)

**From the cockpit.** Open the **CockpitUrl** from your event outputs. The
**Hackathon helper** panel is already open on the right; if you closed it,
press **Ask the helper** in the top bar. Type a question and press **Ask**.
Every answer carries a link to its trace and to its ledger record.

![The cockpit's Hackathon helper panel: the helper's answer with Trace and Ledger links](/static/images/helper/cockpit-help-panel.png)

It helps only with this workshop environment. For anything else it points you
to the page, a facilitator, or the AWS documentation. If the helper and the
page disagree, the page wins; tell a facilitator.

:::alert{type="info" header="Your questions to the helper are recorded"}
Every question is a governed agent call recorded in the evidence ledger
(prompt summary and run id) and the gateway log. Do not paste secrets into
the helper. Facilitators may read helper conversations for support, never
for judging.
:::

Judging asks for a threshold document dated *before* the runs you present,
and for two named runs whose run ids you wrote down before judging. Modules 5,
7 and 8 all produce runs, so before your first scored run read "What to bring to
judging" in [The Challenge](/challenge-brief), write your thresholds down and
date them.

You know the mission, how you win and the two rules. Next, join your event
and get into your account: [Module 1: Know Your Environment](/environment-setup).
